name: Anabolic diet / high calorie eating

angle.text: The 1990s Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic bodybuilding plan, grouped with heavy-eating approaches to gaining size. It is promoted for building muscle, and no studies of its appearance results were found.

summary: A cyclic low-carbohydrate bodybuilding diet from the 1990s, often grouped with heavy-eating approaches to gaining size; no appearance studies found.
note: Sources for this entry are thin; no community discussion or trials were found.
currentQuick:
The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet described in a 1995 book by Mauro Di Pasquale, a Canadian powerlifter and writer. It was nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet.
It is grouped here with high-calorie eating for size. Little material specific to appearance was found, so this entry is short.
How it works: The diet is described as a cyclic ketogenic approach that alternates low-carbohydrate eating with higher-carbohydrate periods. Details of the claimed mechanism are not covered in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: No clinical studies were found, and the sources reviewed do not document risks specific to the diet.
deepLead:
The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet (CKD) published in 1995 by Mauro Di Pasquale, and it was nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet . Di Pasquale, born in 1945, is an Italian-born Canadian powerlifter and writer who won the IPF World Powerlifting Championships in 1976 and later worked as an anti-doping figure in professional wrestling .
Heavy or high-calorie eating more broadly refers to eating a large calorie surplus to gain weight and muscle, a practice covered under bulking . No studies found test the Anabolic Diet for appearance outcomes.

name: Beef organ / liver diet

angle.text: Followers eat beef liver and other organ meats as a dense source of vitamins and minerals, a trend spread partly by fitness influencers. Users link this to better training and general condition; its use for appearance is anecdotal.

summary: Eating beef liver and other organ meats for nutrients; liver is very nutrient-dense but also very high in preformed vitamin A.
note: Liver supplies preformed vitamin A at levels that can exceed the tolerable upper intake from a single serving; no appearance studies found.
currentQuick:
Organ meats such as liver, heart and kidney are eaten in many cuisines and are sometimes promoted by fitness influencers for their nutrient density. This entry concerns eating them for general nutrition and appearance-related goals.
No human trials found test the practice for appearance. Food-science studies have examined adding organs to ground beef patties.
How it works: Liver is described as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and preformed vitamin A, and as very high in vitamin B12.
Risks and caveats: Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A, with effects on bone, liver and the nervous system, and birth risks in pregnancy. A single slice of beef liver can exceed the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A.
deepLead:
Offal, or organ meat, refers to the internal organs of butchered animals such as liver, heart, kidney, tongue and tripe . Attitudes vary: some cultures treat it as taboo and others eat it daily or as a delicacy, and Wikipedia notes that awareness of its nutritional value has grown in places like Ireland, partly through fitness influencers .
Animal liver is described as rich in iron, copper, B vitamins and preformed vitamin A, and as very high in vitamin B12 . The same source states that a single 68 g slice of beef liver exceeds the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A .
No human studies found test an organ-meat or liver diet for appearance outcomes.

name: Deltoid / shoulder implants

angle.text: Discussed in hardmaxxing circles as a surgical way to add width and roundness to the shoulders for a V-shaped upper body. The contour change would be visible directly; research found is on joint replacement, not cosmetic use.

summary: Surgical shoulder-contour implants are talked about for width, but no cosmetic studies exist; the research is all joint replacement.
note: Surgical procedure; published implant research concerns joint replacement, not appearance.
currentQuick:
The idea is to place an implant to make the shoulders look broader or rounder. It is discussed as a surgical route to the wide-shoulder look.
No published study of implants used purely for shoulder appearance was found. Shoulder implant research covers joint replacement for medical conditions.
How it works: An implant would add volume over the deltoid or shoulder region, changing the outline. The deltoid itself is the muscle that rounds the shoulder contour.
Risks and caveats: As with any surgical implant, complications such as infection are documented in the joint-replacement literature, but the risks of a cosmetic shoulder implant have not been studied in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Deltoid or shoulder implants, in the context of looksmaxxing, refers to the idea of surgically placing a solid implant over or within the shoulder region to increase the apparent width or roundness of the shoulders. The deltoid is the muscle that forms the rounded contour of the shoulder and is the prime mover of arm abduction . Broad shoulders are among the proportions discussed in appearance communities as part of a V-shaped upper body.
Published research located for this entry does not describe cosmetic deltoid implants. The surgical literature on shoulder implants concerns joint replacement (arthroplasty) for arthritis, fractures and rotator cuff disease, which is a different purpose and procedure . No clinical study of implants placed solely to enlarge the shoulder contour was found, so this article is deliberately short.

name: Padded shoulders / structured jackets

angle.text: Padded shoulders and structured jackets add visible width and a more athletic silhouette immediately, with no training or surgery. Users also say pads visually straighten sloping clavicles. The look is backed by fashion history rather than attractiveness studies.

summary: Padded shoulders and structured jackets fake shoulder width with tailoring; fashion history backs the look, but no studies test attractiveness effects.
note: No appearance studies; sports-pad research is about protection, not looks.
currentQuick:
Pads and structured tailoring extend the shoulder line so the shoulders look broader and the torso more V-shaped. Fashion has used the effect repeatedly since the 1930s.
In forums some users report positive reactions, while others prefer building muscle instead. No controlled studies exist.
How it works: Padding sewn into a jacket, or inserts worn on the shoulder, add volume beyond the natural frame and hold a firm outline.
Risks and caveats: No health risks were documented for fashion padding in the sources reviewed. Sports shoulder pads studied in research are a separate product with heat-stress and injury literature.
deepLead:
Padded shoulders and structured jackets are a clothing approach used to make the shoulders appear broader and the torso more V-shaped. Fashion shoulder pads are fabric-covered padding sewn inside garments to broaden the look of the shoulders and reduce the appearance of slope . In looksmaxxing communities the practice is discussed as a way to add optical shoulder width without training or surgery.
No studies measuring how padded tailoring changes perceived attractiveness were found. The evidence here is historical and anecdotal: fashion history documents repeated cycles of padded-shoulder styles , and forum users describe their own experiences .

name: Horizontal stripes and layering for width

angle.text: People wear horizontal stripes and layers to look broader across the chest and shoulders; layers add real volume and stripes are said to draw the eye sideways. The visual effect is immediate, and no direct studies were found.

summary: Wearing horizontal stripes and layers to look broader is a styling tactic with no direct studies behind it.
note: No research on clothing stripes and perceived body width was found.
currentQuick:
People use horizontal patterns and stacked layers to make the chest and shoulders look wider or bulkier. Layers genuinely add volume.
The stripe effect itself has not been tested in the sources reviewed; related illusion research uses line drawings, not clothing.
How it works: Horizontal patterns are said to lead the eye across the body, and layers add fabric thickness around the torso.
Risks and caveats: No health risks apply. The main caveat is that the perceptual effect on clothed bodies has not been measured here.
deepLead:
Horizontal stripes and layering are clothing techniques that people in looksmaxxing communities use to make the upper body look broader or bulkier. Layered garments add real volume, and horizontal patterns are said to draw the eye sideways across the chest and shoulders.
Searching for supporting research found nothing specific to this practice. The related perceptual literature on the vertical-horizontal illusion concerns line judgments, not clothing, and no clinical studies of stripes or layering on perceived body width were found .

name: Gymnastic rings

angle.text: Suspended rings are used for bodyweight training, with the gymnast physique as the draw. Men's still rings is a strength-heavy gymnastics event. No studies compare rings for looks.

summary: Suspended rings for bodyweight training; the gymnast physique is the draw, but no studies compare them for looks.
note: Training-specific evidence is lacking; calisthenics research is general.
currentQuick:
Gymnastic rings are straps with rings you hang from a frame or bar to do dips, levers and muscle-ups. They are the apparatus behind gymnasts' upper-body strength.
Research on calisthenics in general is mildly positive for strength and body composition, but rings themselves have not been compared with other tools for appearance.
How it works: Because the rings move freely, bodyweight exercises on them require extra stabilization from the shoulders and arms.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to rings were found in the sources reviewed. Advanced skills such as the iron cross are demanding strength elements in competition.
deepLead:
Gymnastic rings are a pair of rings suspended from a frame by straps, used both as an artistic gymnastics apparatus and as a bodyweight training tool. In competition the still rings event is traditionally performed only by male gymnasts because of its demand for upper-body strength . In calisthenics, rings can be used for dips, front and back levers and muscle-ups .
In looksmaxxing, rings are mentioned as a way to build the upper body physique associated with gymnasts. No trials were found that test rings against other training tools for appearance outcomes.

name: Fat Gripz / grip thickeners

angle.text: Users attach thick rubber sleeves to bars and dumbbells to challenge grip and forearms for arm size. One acute study exists, and none examine forearm size or appearance.

summary: Thick rubber grip sleeves sold for forearm work; one acute study exists, none on forearm size.
note: No long-term data on forearm thickness.
currentQuick:
Fat Gripz wrap around a bar to make it thicker so the hands and forearms work harder when holding it. They are marketed for forearm thickening.
Only one acute study on strength and muscle activation was found; forearm growth has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
How it works: A thicker handle reduces how well the fingers can wrap around it, increasing the demand on the grip muscles.
Risks and caveats: No adverse effects were documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Fat Gripz are thick rubber sleeves that attach to a barbell, dumbbell or handle to increase its diameter, making it harder to hold. They are used in strength training with the aim of challenging grip and forearm muscles.
One study examined the acute effects of Fat Gripz on muscle activation and strength in 15 resistance-trained men . The sources available here give no data on long-term forearm size changes, so this article is brief.

name: EMS suit / electrical muscle stimulation

angle.text: Whole-body EMS suits are sold for fitness and toning on the idea that stimulated contractions build muscle. EMS is established in rehab and small fitness trials exist; its effect on looks is untested.

summary: Electrodes that make muscles contract; real in rehab, small trials in fitness, nothing on looks, with rare serious harms reported.
note: Rhabdomyolysis case reported after whole-body sessions; contraindicated with pacemakers.
currentQuick:
EMS uses electrical pulses to trigger muscle contractions, and whole-body suits do this across many muscles during a workout. It is established in rehabilitation and marketed for fitness.
Small trials in healthy adults exist, but none found here measure muscle appearance.
How it works: Pulses through skin electrodes depolarize motor nerves and make muscle fibers contract, and are said to recruit fast-twitch fibers [1].
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation and burns are listed adverse effects, pacemakers and several conditions are contraindications, and a case of rhabdomyolysis after whole-body EMS has been reported.
deepLead:
Electrical muscle stimulation (EMS, also called NMES or electromyostimulation) uses electrical impulses delivered through skin electrodes to make muscles contract, and is used in rehabilitation, athletic training and consumer fitness . Whole-body EMS suits apply electrodes across many muscle groups at once and are sold commercially for fitness.
Small randomized trials of whole-body EMS in healthy adults exist , and a Danish case report describes rhabdomyolysis after a whole-body session . No trial found here measures muscle appearance as an outcome.

name: Gynecomastia surgery

angle.text: Men use male breast reduction to remove glandular tissue and fat for a flatter chest, which suits shirtless and fitted-clothing looks. The change is visible directly. It is the established medical route when enlargement persists.

summary: Surgical removal of excess glandular and fatty chest tissue in men; the established medical route when enlargement persists, with documented complication risks and variable insurance coverage.
note: Surgical procedure with documented complications such as hematoma, asymmetry and altered sensation; often classed as cosmetic by insurers.
currentQuick:
Gynecomastia is enlargement of glandular breast tissue in males. Surgery removes that tissue, often combined with liposuction of surrounding fat, to flatten the chest contour. Reference sources describe it as the main treatment when the condition persists beyond about a year, is distressing, and has become fibrotic.
In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a chest-contouring procedure, and clinical studies have examined its effect on quality of life, particularly in adolescents and young men.
How it works: Techniques described in the literature include subcutaneous mastectomy through a small incision around the areola, liposuction-assisted removal, and laser-assisted variants. The aim is to remove glandular tissue, which liposuction alone may not address.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, seroma, asymmetry, altered nipple or breast sensation, visible scarring, contour irregularities and, rarely, nipple or areola necrosis. Many US insurers classify the procedure as cosmetic and deny coverage. Pubertal gynecomastia often resolves on its own, so surgery in teenagers is generally deferred.
deepLead:
Gynecomastia surgery, also called male breast reduction, is a set of operations that remove excess glandular tissue and, often, fat from the male chest. Gynecomastia itself results from an altered balance between estrogen and androgen activity and can arise during puberty, in older age, with certain medications or illnesses, or without an identified cause .
Reference sources describe surgery as considered when enlargement has persisted for roughly a year or more, causes physical or psychological distress, and has become fibrotic, and as typically reserved for cases that do not respond to medication . A professional body cited on Wikipedia calls surgery the most effective known treatment for the condition . Published case series and database analyses have documented complication rates and patient-reported outcomes .
Clinical studies of the operation consist largely of observational series, comparisons of technique and quality-of-life questionnaires, plus a number of small registered trials of specific methods .

name: Chin tucks

angle.text: Users do chin tucks to improve head posture and, in some accounts, to sharpen the jaw and neck line. Research mostly concerns swallowing therapy and neck muscle activity; the jawline use is based on anecdote.

summary: A neck-retraction movement used for posture and deep neck flexor work; most published research concerns swallowing therapy, not jawline appearance.
note: Research on chin tucks is mainly from swallowing studies; some forum users warn about prolonged holds.
currentQuick:
A chin tuck is a movement in which the head is drawn straight back so the chin moves toward the neck without tilting the head down. It is used in posture routines and aimed at the deep neck flexor muscles, and it is often paired in forums with rows and face pulls for forward head posture.
Published studies of chin tucks are mostly in swallowing (dysphagia) research, where the posture is used as a compensatory maneuver. Studies of its effect on facial appearance were not found.
How it works: Proponents say the movement strengthens the deep neck flexors and counteracts a head carried forward of the shoulders, which they link to a more defined jaw-neck profile. Swallowing studies show that the chin-tuck posture changes pharyngeal dimensions and pressure events.
Risks and caveats: No serious harms are documented in the sources reviewed. One looksmax.org thread author claims that holding a chin tuck for long periods could strain the cervical spine, a claim that other users in the thread called fear mongering; no study cited here tests it.
deepLead:
A chin tuck is a posture or exercise in which the head is retracted backward over the neck so that the chin draws in. In clinical literature the term most often refers to a swallowing maneuver used with people who have dysphagia, and it has been studied with videofluoroscopy and manometry . A resisted version, chin tuck against resistance (CTAR), was proposed as a way to increase activity of the suprahyoid muscles .
In looksmaxxing communities the movement is discussed in connection with posture and head position, in the belief that a head held forward weakens the appearance of the jawline and neck. Forward head posture is described by Wikipedia as a common postural pattern linked to prolonged device use, with deep neck flexor strengthening among the proposed remedies . No clinical study located here has measured whether chin tucks change facial or jaw appearance.

name: Wall angels

angle.text: Used in posture routines to improve shoulder and upper-back mobility for a straighter, more open stance. It is common in rehab and fitness; no appearance trials were found.

summary: A wall-supported arm-slide drill used for shoulder and upper back mobility and posture; popular in rehab and fitness, with no appearance trials found.
note: Described in fitness sources as a mobility drill; no clinical studies of it were located for appearance or posture change.
currentQuick:
Wall angels are a bodyweight drill in which a person stands with the back against a wall and slides the arms up and down while keeping the head, upper back, hips, elbows and hands in contact. It is described as a shoulder mobility and scapular control exercise used in physical therapy, Pilates and general fitness.
In posture-focused looksmaxxing circles it is grouped with chest stretches and rowing movements as a way to counter rounded shoulders from desk work. No published trial located here tests wall angels for posture or appearance.
How it works: Fitness sources say the movement stretches the chest muscles while engaging the rhomboids, trapezius, serratus anterior and rotator cuff and encouraging thoracic extension. These are proposed mechanisms rather than demonstrated outcomes.
Risks and caveats: The exercise needs only a wall and is described as scalable, with advice to reduce range if pain occurs. No harms are documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Wall angels, also called wall slides or the V-to-W stretch, are a standing bodyweight exercise in which the arms are slid up and down a wall while the head, upper back, buttocks, elbows and hands stay in contact with it .
Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, describes them as part of physical therapy, Pilates and postural routines meant to counter rounded shoulders and shortened chest muscles from sitting and desk work, and says they target shoulder mobility, scapular stability and thoracic flexibility . Those descriptions are not backed in the source by clinical trials, and no study of wall angels specifically was found.

name: Thoracic extension over foam roller

angle.text: Users do this mobility drill to counter rounded posture and stiffness, aiming for a more upright look. It appears in posture routines; no trials of the drill itself were found.

summary: A mobility drill that arches the upper back over a foam roller, used to counter rounded posture; no trials of the drill itself were found.
note: Related literature covers thoracic manipulation and sitting posture, not this specific drill.
currentQuick:
The drill involves lying with a foam roller under the upper back and extending the thoracic spine over it. It is discussed in posture routines aimed at rounded upper back and forward head carriage.
No clinical study of the foam-roller drill was located. Related research examines thoracic manipulation for neck pain and the muscle activity in different sitting postures.
How it works: Proponents say it mobilizes stiff thoracic joints so the upper back can extend and the shoulders and head sit further back. This is a proposed mechanism not demonstrated by trials of the drill.
Risks and caveats: No harms are documented in the sources reviewed; people with spinal conditions are generally referred to clinicians for exercise advice.
deepLead:
Thoracic extension over a foam roller is a self-mobilization exercise in which the upper back is arched back over a roller. It is used in posture-focused routines for stiffness and a flexed upper back.
Wikipedia describes forward head posture as associated with a hunched thoracic spine and lists thoracic mobilization among proposed remedies, citing a randomized trial in which thoracic manipulation reduced neck pain immediately; it also notes that some of its treatment claims need better sourcing . That trial studied clinician-delivered manipulation, not foam-roller self-mobilization.

name: Hip flexor stretching (couch stretch)

angle.text: The couch stretch is used in posture circles to loosen the hip flexors and counter anterior pelvic tilt for a flatter-looking stomach and better stance. It is popular, with no trials on that use.

summary: A kneeling quad-and-hip-flexor stretch used to counter anterior pelvic tilt; popular in posture circles, with no trials on that use.
note: Research covers flexibility and performance, not pelvic tilt or appearance.
currentQuick:
The couch stretch holds the rear hip in extension with the knee bent to lengthen the hip flexors and front thigh. It is widely recommended in posture and looksmaxxing communities as a fix for anterior pelvic tilt.
Trials of hip flexor stretching have looked at flexibility and athletic performance. No study found tests it for pelvic tilt or appearance.
How it works: The stretch is thought to lengthen the iliopsoas and rectus femoris, which proponents say pull the pelvis forward when shortened by long periods of sitting.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are documented. The position loads the knee and hip, and general guidance advises people with joint problems to seek clinical advice.
deepLead:
Hip flexor stretching is a flexibility practice aimed at the muscles at the front of the hip, chiefly the iliopsoas and the rectus femoris of the quadriceps. The couch stretch is a popular variation in which the rear knee is placed on the floor with the shin braced up against a couch, wall or bench, so that the hip is held in extension while the front of the thigh is lengthened. 
In looksmaxxing and posture circles the stretch is discussed mainly as a way to reduce anterior pelvic tilt, a posture in which the front of the pelvis drops relative to the back. Proponents attribute this pattern partly to shortened hip flexors from prolonged sitting. 
Published research on hip flexor stretching has mostly looked at flexibility and athletic performance rather than pelvic posture or facial and body appearance. A 2021 systematic review with meta-analysis examined stretching of the hip flexors and performance parameters, and a small laboratory study examined hip extension range of motion and vertical jump.  No trial found in this search tests the couch stretch specifically as a treatment for anterior pelvic tilt.

name: Glute bridges / glute activation

angle.text: Glute bridges are used to strengthen the glutes and, in posture circles, to counter anterior pelvic tilt for a flatter lower-back line. They also build glute size. Evidence for the posture use is absent.

summary: A hip-lift exercise used to strengthen the glutes and, in posture circles, to counter anterior pelvic tilt; evidence for that use is absent.
note: Muscle-activation research exists; pelvic tilt and appearance outcomes are untested.
currentQuick:
Lying on the back with bent knees, the person lifts the hips by squeezing the glutes. It is a staple of posture routines aimed at anterior pelvic tilt.
Wikipedia lists it among suggested exercises but flags the sourcing as weak. No trial tests it for pelvic tilt or looks.
How it works: The glutes extend the hip. Proponents say strengthening them helps hold the pelvis in a more neutral position.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are documented for bodyweight bridges. Back or hip pain is typically referred to a clinician.
deepLead:
The glute bridge is a floor exercise in which a person lies on their back with knees bent and lifts the hips by contracting the gluteal and hamstring muscles. Related bridge exercises are described by Wikipedia as intended to improve lower back and gluteus strength.  The term glute activation refers to low-load drills such as bridges that are used to switch on the gluteal muscles before heavier training.
In looksmaxxing and posture communities the glute bridge is listed as a counter to anterior pelvic tilt, on the idea that weak glutes allow the pelvis to tip forward.  Wikipedia's article on pelvic tilt lists glute bridges among recommended exercises, but flags that part of the article as relying on a consumer-health source. 
No clinical trial of glute bridges as a treatment for pelvic tilt or for appearance was found.

name: Anterior pelvic tilt correction

chain: Stretch hips, strengthen glutes and core
angle.text: Proponents use this routine to reduce pelvic tilt, citing a flatter-looking stomach, better posture and in some accounts more apparent height. It is widely recommended online and is thinly referenced and untested for looks.

summary: A stretch-and-strengthen routine aimed at tipping the pelvis back to neutral; widely recommended online, thinly referenced and untested for looks.
note: Sources note weak referencing; persistent back pain warrants clinical assessment.
currentQuick:
APT correction bundles hip flexor stretches with glute and core exercises to reduce forward pelvic tilt and the lower-back arch. Proponents cite better posture, a flatter stomach and sometimes more apparent height.
Encyclopedic sources describe the same approach but flag weak referencing. No controlled study tests it for appearance.
How it works: The idea is that shortened hip flexors and weak glutes and abdominals pull the pelvis forward, so lengthening the former and strengthening the latter rebalances it.
Risks and caveats: Exercise itself is low risk, but hyperlordosis can accompany back pain, disc problems or structural conditions that a clinician would assess.
deepLead:
Anterior pelvic tilt (APT) is described as a posture in which the front of the pelvis drops relative to the back, often accompanied by an exaggerated lower-back arch known as lumbar hyperlordosis.  In looksmaxxing and fitness communities, APT correction refers to a package of stretches and strengthening exercises intended to reduce that tilt, with proponents citing a flatter-looking stomach, better posture and, in some accounts, increased apparent height. 
The usual package is hip flexor stretching, glute strengthening and core work such as glute bridges, planks, side planks and dead bugs.  Wikipedia notes that this recommendation relies on a consumer-health source and that the article needs better references. 
Medical sources describe lumbar hyperlordosis as associated with prolonged sitting, weak abdominal and gluteal muscles, tight hip flexors and hamstrings, excess visceral fat and pregnancy, as well as structural conditions.  No controlled trial found tests an APT correction program for appearance.

name: Core stability (plank, dead bug)

angle.text: Planks and dead bugs are pitched for posture and pelvic tilt and to firm the midsection. Core-stability research shows modest benefit over general exercise; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: Plank and dead bug trunk drills pitched for posture and pelvic tilt; broader core-stability research shows modest benefit over general exercise.
note: Wikipedia notes limited research support for the core stability model.
currentQuick:
Core stability training uses holds like the plank and controlled movements like the dead bug to train the trunk. Posture communities include it in pelvic tilt routines.
Encyclopedic sources say research support for the core stability model is limited, and nothing found tests it for appearance.
How it works: The exercises train the abdominal, back and hip muscles to hold the spine and pelvis in position under load or movement.
Risks and caveats: Generally low risk. Back pain during exercise is usually referred to a clinician.
deepLead:
Core stability is defined as a person's ability to control the tone, position and movement of the core, meaning the head, neck and torso.  The plank, an isometric hold resembling a push-up position, and the dead bug, a lying limb-movement drill, are common training exercises for it. 
In looksmaxxing and posture communities, core stability work is recommended as part of correcting anterior pelvic tilt and improving trunk posture.  Wikipedia lists planks, side planks and dead bugs among exercises suggested for that purpose, while flagging weak sourcing. 
Wikipedia states that there is little research support for the core stability model and that core-specific training performs about as well as general exercise at best, and cites a critical review titled "The myth of core stability".  Whether core training changes pelvic tilt or appearance has not been tested in studies found.

name: McGill Big 3

angle.text: This three-exercise core routine from spine biomechanist Stuart McGill is used for back-sparing trunk strength and, in posture circles, for better carriage. Its use for looks is untested.

summary: A three-exercise back-sparing core routine tied to biomechanist Stuart McGill; thinly documented here and untested for looks.
note: Little source material; no appearance outcomes studied.
currentQuick:
The Big 3 are a curl-up, side bridge and bird dog associated with spine researcher Stuart McGill, used for trunk endurance with low spinal load.
Posture communities fold it into pelvic tilt and back routines. No study found tests it for appearance.
How it works: The exercises are described as training abdominal and back muscles to stabilise the spine without bending it repeatedly.
Risks and caveats: Low risk in general; back pain is usually referred to a clinician.
deepLead:
The McGill Big 3 is a trio of core exercises, usually described as a modified curl-up, the side bridge and the bird dog, associated with spine biomechanist Stuart McGill. McGill is a Canadian academic and Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo, a member of the Order of Canada since 2019 and the author of books including Low Back Disorders and Back Mechanic. 
The routine is promoted as a way to build trunk endurance while limiting load on the spine, and in posture and looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes included in routines for anterior pelvic tilt and back health. 
The sources loaded for this article describe McGill's academic role but do not detail the Big 3 exercises or trials of them, so this article is short. No study found tests the Big 3 for pelvic tilt or appearance.

name: Lower trap / serratus work

angle.text: Exercises for the lower trapezius and serratus anterior are used in posture routines to hold the shoulder blades in place for a more open upper body. The anatomy is well described; the appearance benefit is untested.

summary: Exercises for the shoulder-blade muscles used in posture routines; anatomy is well described, appearance benefit untested.
note: Sources cover anatomy and nerve injury, not training outcomes.
currentQuick:
The lower trapezius and serratus anterior steer the shoulder blade. Posture communities train them to counter rounded shoulders.
Anatomy sources describe their roles; no study found tests this training for posture or looks.
How it works: The lower trapezius depresses and rotates the scapula and the serratus anterior pulls it around the ribcage, together stabilising it during arm movement.
Risks and caveats: Low risk in general. Persistent winging or shoulder pain can reflect nerve injury and is a clinical matter.
deepLead:
Lower trapezius and serratus anterior work refers to exercises aimed at the muscles that control the shoulder blade (scapula). The lower trapezius pulls the scapula down and helps rotate it upward, while the serratus anterior pulls it forward around the rib cage; together with the upper trapezius they sustain upward rotation for overhead arm movement. 
In posture and looksmaxxing circles these muscles are discussed in connection with rounded shoulders and upper-back posture, with proponents saying that stronger scapular stabilisers support a more upright appearance. 
The encyclopedic sources describe anatomy and nerve-injury problems such as winged scapula, not trials of strengthening for posture or looks. No clinical study found tests the practice for appearance.

name: Rib flare correction / diaphragm breathing

angle.text: Posture communities use diaphragm breathing and core drills to pull protruding lower ribs back for a cleaner torso line. Proponents link rib flare to weak core and breathing mechanics; direct trials on appearance are almost absent.

summary: Breathing and core drills aimed at pulling protruding lower ribs back in; popular in posture circles, with almost no direct trial evidence on appearance.
note: A visibly prominent rib cage can also reflect structural conditions (scoliosis, pectus), which breathing drills are not described as treating.
currentQuick:
Rib flare describes lower ribs that stick out forward or sideways, most visible in side view or when the arms are raised. Fitness and physical-therapy writers commonly link it to posture, core weakness and chest-dominant breathing, and looksmaxxing forums discuss it as something that can spoil the torso silhouette.
The correction approach centres on diaphragmatic breathing and core-bracing drills meant to lower the rib cage over the pelvis. Descriptions come largely from physical-therapy and fitness sources; no controlled trial found tests breathing drills for changing visible rib prominence in otherwise healthy people.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is that the diaphragm and deep abdominal muscles control how the lower ribs sit. Proponents say retraining exhalation and core engagement restores the contact zone between diaphragm and ribs and lets the ribs rest lower. A related clinical-commentary literature describes asymmetrical rib and pelvic positioning treated with specific respiratory exercises.
Risks and caveats: The exercises themselves are low-impact and generally regarded as low risk. The main caveat reported in the sources is that flared or prominent ribs can accompany scoliosis, pectus excavatum or other structural conditions, which are assessed by clinicians and managed differently, including surgically in some pectus cases.
deepLead:
Rib flare is a descriptive term, used mainly in physical therapy, fitness and posture communities, for lower ribs that protrude outward or forward rather than sitting flush with the abdomen. It is generally described as a postural pattern rather than a disease, although similar-looking rib cage prominence can accompany structural conditions such as scoliosis or pectus excavatum.
Rib flare correction refers to exercises, chiefly diaphragmatic breathing combined with core engagement and posture work, intended to bring the lower ribs down and back. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed alongside pectus excavatum as a torso-aesthetics concern.
No clinical trial found has tested breathing exercises specifically for reducing visible rib flare. Related literature consists of radiographic measurement studies of rib cage deformity in scoliosis, clinical commentary on respiratory exercises for asymmetrical trunk posture, and surgical series on pectus repair.

name: Jefferson curl

angle.text: Popular in strength circles as a mobility exercise for the spine and hamstrings, sometimes tied to posture. It has barely been studied, with one small 2026 EMG study, and its appearance use is anecdotal.

summary: A loaded spinal-flexion mobility exercise popular in strength circles; barely studied, with one small 2026 EMG study to date.
note: Deliberately loads the spine in flexion, a position many clinicians and lifters treat cautiously; published research is minimal.
currentQuick:
The Jefferson curl is a strength and mobility exercise in which a person slowly rolls the spine into flexion while holding a light weight, then returns to standing. It is discussed in strength-training, rehabilitation and posture communities as a way to build hamstring and back flexibility and posterior-chain tolerance.
Research is very thin. A 2026 study characterised erector spinae muscle activity during the exercise compared with the Romanian deadlift, and described the exercise as popular but lacking empirical characterisation. No trial found tests it for posture or appearance outcomes.
How it works: Proponents say gradual loaded flexion through a controlled range increases flexibility and conditions the spine's tissues. Researchers have so far only measured muscle activation during the movement and compared it with a hip-hinge lift.
Risks and caveats: Loaded spinal flexion is a movement pattern that some clinicians and coaches advise caution with, particularly for people with back pain. A qualitative study of people with chronic low back pain found participants perceiving some exercises as potentially injurious. No injury-rate data specific to the Jefferson curl were found.
deepLead:
The Jefferson curl is a loaded spinal flexion exercise in which the lifter, standing with a weight, progressively curls the spine forward and down vertebra by vertebra and then reverses the movement. A 2026 paper describes it as having gained popularity in strength and rehabilitation practice but lacking empirical characterisation.
In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is sometimes grouped with mobility work for the posterior chain. The only study identified is a cross-sectional surface electromyography (EMG) study in resistance-trained adults comparing erector spinae activation during the Jefferson curl with a Romanian deadlift at a matched submaximal load. No trial has examined effects on posture or visible appearance.
